questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/799fd5d6528a9a66060d47e8f7613643ee5a305ed0dc494fabc1fc0ecf089e84.png)

The graph of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ is shown above. The points $A,B,$ and $C$ lie on the curve and have $x$-coordinates $x=-3,$ $x=0,$ and $x=3.$ Given that ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at $A,B,$ and $C,$ find the intervals where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We have ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

The information about ${f}^{′}(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,-3) & -3 & (-3,0) & 0 & (0,3) & 3 & (3,\infty ) \\ f & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ & \text{no extr.} & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & + & 0 & - & 0 & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ on the intervals $(-\infty ,-3)$ and $(3,\infty ).$

questions.problem:
Given that $g(x)=3{x}^{4}-8{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+1$ is defined for $x\in (-8,8),$ find the values of $x$ for which the function is strictly decreasing.

$x\in (${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =12{x}^{3}-24{x}^{2}+12x \\  & =12x({x}^{2}-2x+1) \\  & =12x{(x-1)}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
12x{(x-1)}^{2}<0.
$$

Since $(x-1)^{2}\ge 0$ for all real $x$, the sign of $12x{(x-1)}^{2}$ is determined by the sign of $12x$, so $12x{(x-1)}^{2}<0$ exactly when $12x<0.$ This yields

$$
\begin{aligned}12x & <0 \\ x & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is restricted to $x\in (-8,8),$ we conclude that $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $x\in (-8,0).$

questions.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)={e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}$ is strictly decreasing.
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)={e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}(4x-6),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}(4x-6)<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The exponential function is always positive, so this reduces to

$$
4x-6<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-6 & <0 \\ 4x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,\frac{3}{2}).$

questions.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=4{x}^{3}-27{x}^{2}-30x+9$ is strictly decreasing.
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =12{x}^{2}-54x-30 \\  & =6(2{x}^{2}-9x-5),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
6(2{x}^{2}-9x-5)<0.
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
6(2x+1)(x-5)<0,
$$

and the graph of $y=6(2x+1)(x-5)$ has roots at $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=5,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/7eec3fc84b851b3b39e5ae8ecff1343f39393d1dd8f7a6cce8e8904dc1c65d48.png)

The graph is negative on the interval $(-\frac{1}{2},5)$ between the roots, so we conclude that ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ on the interval $(-\frac{1}{2},5).$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\frac{1}{2},5).$

questions.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)$ is strictly decreasing.
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 4x \\  & =\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1}<0.
$$

The function $2{x}^{2}+1$ is always positive. So, this reduces to

$$
4x<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & <0 \\ x & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,0).$

questions.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=5-7x-4{x}^{2}$ is strictly decreasing.
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-7-8x \\  & =-8(x+\frac{7}{8}),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
-8(x+\frac{7}{8})<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8(x+\frac{7}{8}) & <0 \\ 0 & <8(x+\frac{7}{8}) \\ 0 & <x+\frac{7}{8} \\ -\frac{7}{8} & <x.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $x\in (-\frac{7}{8},\infty ).$

questions.problem:
Find the values of $x$ for which the function $g(x)=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{7}{4}{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x+1$ is strictly increasing.

$x<$
{{field-1}} $\,$ and $\,x>$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${g}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & ={x}^{2}-\frac{7}{2}x+\frac{3}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
{x}^{2}-\frac{7}{2}x+\frac{3}{2}>0.
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
(x-\frac{1}{2})(x-3)>0.
$$

The graph of $y=(x-\frac{1}{2})(x-3)$ has roots at $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=3,$ as shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/26374f7e5c86c5585d384b3e65b4a1b3fb2f94172ed753cdb3fe7bdb0af0abb8.png)

For an upward-opening parabola, the product $(x-\frac{1}{2})(x-3)$ is positive when $x<\frac{1}{2}$ or $x>3.$

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the intervals 

$$
x<\frac{1}{2}\,\text{and}\,x>3.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/61b89de34a6900d2ea39e5c2af141b3353e9ca790ac2748d0fc6d4d578127f93.png)

Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ (plotted above) is strictly increasing.
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x)$ using the product  rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}\cdot x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1>0.
$$

Solving $\operatorname{ln}⁡x=-1$ gives the critical point

$$
x={e}^{-1}\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{e}.
$$

From the graph, we see that this critical point is a minimum. We also see that the slope of the tangent lines is negative to the left of the critical point and positive to the right of the critical point. 

So, we summarize the sign of the derivative in the following table:

$$
\left.\begin{aligned}x & (0,\frac{1}{e}) & \frac{1}{e} & (\frac{1}{e},\infty ) \\ f & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}\right|
$$

Finally, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the interval $(\frac{1}{e},\infty ).$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{3}+\frac{3}{x}$ is defined for $x\in (0,\infty ),$ find the values of $x$ for which the function is strictly increasing.
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}>0.
$$

Using that $x>0,$ the above inequality factors as

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} & >0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & >0 \\ {x}^{2}({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) & >0 \\ {x}^{4}-1 & >0 \\ ({x}^{2}+1)(x+1)(x-1) & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

The factors ${x}^{2}+1$ and $x+1$ are positive, so this reduces to

$$
x-1>0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & >0 \\ x & >1.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $(1,\infty ).$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})$ is defined for $x\in (-2\pi ,0),$ find the values of $x$ for which the function is strictly increasing.
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the domain is $x\in (-2\pi ,0),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\pi  & <x<0 \\ -\pi  & <\frac{x}{2}<0.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that cosine is positive in the first and the fourth quadrant. So, this reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{\pi }{2} & <\frac{x}{2}<0 \\ -\pi  & <x<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on the interval $-\pi <x<0.$

canonical_examples.problem:
The graph of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ is shown below. The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the curve and have $x$-coordinates $x=1$ and $x=4.$ Given that $f'(x) = 0$ at both $A$ and $B,$ find the intervals where $f'(x)>0.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/1a8208a75b7df62a0c692e08f74509ecf1462e3ab1f8dd7eae85a56272abde48.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We have $f'(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then $f'(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then $f'(x)<0.$

The information about $f'(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,1) & 1 & (1,4) & 4 & (4,+\infty ) \\ f & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ \\ {f}^{′} & - & 0 & + & 0 & -\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f'(x)>0$ on the interval $(1,4).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Intervals on Which a Function Is Decreasing Using Differentiation
canonical_examples.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 8x$ is strictly decreasing.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find where $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, we need to solve the inequality $f'(x) < 0.$

Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+2x-8,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+2x-8<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
3(x + 2)\left(x -\dfrac 4 3\right) < 0,
$$

and the graph of $y=3(x+2)\left(x -\dfrac 4 3\right)$ has roots at $x=-2$ and $x=\dfrac 4 3,$ as shown below.

The graph is negative on the interval $\left( -2, \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ between the roots, so we conclude that $f'(x) < 0$ on the interval $\left( -2, \dfrac{4}{3} \right).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Intervals on Which a Function Is Increasing Using Differentiation
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln{2x}}{x}$ (plotted below) is strictly increasing.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/2ccb7c95d06c78a1730f9ca46aad9b6f1370050c745f2c1fc9208275670c3649.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find where $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, we need to solve the inequality $f'(x) > 0.$

Differentiating $f(x)$ using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x})\cdot x-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\cdot 1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2x}{{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

 

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\dfrac{1-\ln{2x}}{x^2} > 0.
$$

The denominator is  always positive, so this reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2x>0\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡2x<1.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving $\ln{2x} = 1$ gives the critical point

$$
2x = e\quad \Longrightarrow\quad x = \dfrac{1}{2}e.
$$

From the graph, we see that this critical point is a maximum. We also see that the slope of the tangent lines is positive to the left of the critical point and negative to the right of the critical point. 

We summarize this information in the following table:

$$
\left.\begin{aligned}x & (0,\frac{1}{2}e) & \frac{1}{2}e & (\frac{1}{2}e,\infty ) \\ f & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ \\ {f}^{′} & + & 0 & -\end{aligned}\right|
$$

Finally, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the interval $\left(0,\frac 1 2 e\right),$ which can also be written as $0 < x < \dfrac 1 2 e.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Comparing Slopes of Functions at Different Points
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/aa8ee7171576bc92bb9b6a6730223e2629bc0d6216cb54a7a8a9f51d97985d14.png)

Which of the following statements is true?

- $f'(2.5) < f'(1) < f'(-1)$

- $f'(-1) < f'(1) < f'(2.5)$

- $f'(1) < f'(-1) < f'(2.5)$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the graph, we see that

- the slope of the tangent at $x=-1$ is positive, so $f'(-1) > 0.$

- the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is zero, so $f'(1) = 0.$

- the slope of the tangent at $x=2.5$ is negative, and so $f'(2.5) < 0.$

Therefore, only statement I is correct.
